content: 1. Globally, approximately 10% of all births are preterm, defined as occurring before 37 weeks of gestation (March of Dimes, 2012). 2. Each year, over one million infants die as a direct result of being born preterm (Lawn, 2013). 3. Preterm birth significantly impacts both short-term morbidity and mortality, as well as long-term health and disability outcomes. 4. Short-term complications of preterm birth include respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), retinopathy of prematurity, patent ductus arteriosus, and sepsis (Haram, 2003; Saigal, 2008). 5. RDS arises due to immature lung development and is a leading cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality in preterm infants. 6. Preterm birth predisposes infants to chronic lung disease, such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, which may impair airway function into adulthood (Doyle, 2006; Saigal, 2008). 7. Survivors of preterm birth face increased risks of long-term neurodevelopmental disabilities, including cerebral palsy, intellectual impairments, and visual and hearing deficits (Saigal, 2008; Anderson, 2003; Doyle, 2001; Farooqi, 2006; Wood, 2000). 8. The psychosocial and emotional burden of caring for preterm infants significantly affects families (Saigal, 2000; Singer, 1999). 9. Being born preterm also increases the risk of developing non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes and hypertension, later in life (Hovi, 2007). 10. The incidence of preterm birth is rising in nearly all countries with reliable data (Blencowe, 2012). 11. The highest burden of preterm birth occurs in Africa and Asia, where the availability and use of interventions to mitigate its effects vary widely (Blencowe, 2012; Vogel, 2014). 12. The causes of preterm birth differ by geographical location. 13. In high-income countries, the number of provider-initiated preterm births has been increasing (Blencowe, 2012). 14. In France and the United States, over 30% of preterm births in 2000 were medically indicated (Blondel, 2012; Davidoff, 2006). 15. In lowand middle-income countries, the lack of population-based studies makes it difficult to differentiate the causes of preterm birth. 16. Medically indicated preterm births represent a smaller proportion of all preterm births in lowand middle-income countries compared to spontaneous preterm births (Alhaj, 2010; Nkyekyer, 2006). 17. Up to one-third of all preterm births and up to half of very preterm births are provider-initiated, encompassing urgent, discretionary, iatrogenic, and social reasons (Goldenberg, 2008; Menon, 2008; Steer, 2005). 18. The primary maternal and fetal indications for preterm delivery include maternal pre-eclampsia, antepartum hemorrhage, and chronic or acute fetal compromise, such as fetal distress and severe intrauterine growth restriction (Ananth, 2006). 19. The incidence of medically indicated preterm birth is expected to rise due to increasing maternal disease, particularly in light of global epidemics of diabetes and obesity (Lawn, 2013). 20. The etiology of spontaneous preterm birth is not fully understood but is likely multifactorial (Lawn, 2013). 21. In up to half of cases, the cause of spontaneous preterm birth remains unknown (Menon, 2008). 22. Up to half of spontaneous preterm births occur following preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (Goldenberg, 2008). 23. Multiple pregnancy is another significant risk factor, accounting for approximately 15% to 20% of all preterm births (Goldenberg, 2008). 24. The increasing incidence of multiple pregnancies is largely attributed to advancing maternal age and the use of assisted reproductive techniques (Felberbaum, 2007). 25. Advancing maternal age has also been identified as an independent risk factor for spontaneous preterm birth (Goldenberg, 2008). 26. The distribution of preterm births across gestational ages is not uniform. 27. Only 5% of preterm births occur before 28 weeks of gestation, approximately 15% between 28 and 31 weeks, 20% between 32 and 33 weeks, and 60% to 70% between 34 and 36 weeks (Goldenberg, 2008). 28. These figures can vary depending on geographical location. 29. Recent data from Australia reported an overall preterm birth rate of 7.7%, with 10% occurring at 20 to 27 weeks, 9% at 28 to 31 weeks, and 81% at 32 to 36 weeks of gestation (Hilder, 2014). 30. The risks associated with prematurity are inversely related to gestational age (Saigal, 2008). 31. Significant improvements in the survival rates of preterm infants, particularly those born very preterm, have been attributed to the use of antenatal corticosteroids, surfactant therapy, assisted ventilation, and evolving attitudes toward intensive care (Doyle, 1999; Roberts, 2006; Rojas-Reyes, 2012). 32. Survival rates for preterm infants vary significantly depending on the location of birth. 33. Mortality improvements in high-income countries are most pronounced at extremes of gestation and in infants with extremely low birth weight (Saigal, 2008). 34. Population-based cohort studies in Australia have shown marked improvements in the survival of extremely low birth weight infants, from 25% in 1979 to 80% in 1997 (Doyle, 2001). 35. Similarly, a national cohort study in the UK demonstrated an increase in survival rates for infants born between 22 and 25 weeks of gestation, from 40% in 1995 to 53% in 2006 (Costeloe, 2012). 36. However, this trend is not reflected in low-income countries, where over 90% of very preterm infants (less than 28 weeks of gestation) die within the first few days of life, compared to less than 10% in high-income settings (March of Dimes, 2012). 37. There remains uncertainty regarding the use of antenatal corticosteroids at later gestational ages. 38. This question has gained importance due to the increasing number of cesarean sections performed at term and late preterm gestations (McClure, 2007). 39. Cesarean delivery predisposes neonates to respiratory complications, including RDS and transient tachypnea of the newborn (Hook, 1997; Maisels, 1977; Morrison, 1995). 40. The necessity of antenatal corticosteroids at term is debated, as only approximately 5% of these infants require admission for respiratory distress, and serious morbidity is uncommon (Stutchfield, 2005). 41. Concerns exist regarding the potential long-term adverse effects of corticosteroid exposure in more mature fetuses (Aiken, 2014; Steer, 2005). 42. As the risk of neonatal respiratory complications decreases with advancing gestational age, delaying elective cesarean delivery until 39 weeks or later appears to be an equally effective solution (Al Kiaat, 2013; NICE, 2011; Stutchfield, 2005). 43. Antenatal corticosteroids are recommended by the World Health Organization as a priority intervention to prevent RDS and mortality in preterm infants (PMNCH, 2011; WHO, 2015). 44. However, the use of antenatal corticosteroids in lowand middle-income countries remains low, highlighting an opportunity to improve outcomes for preterm infants through increased administration (Vogel, 2014; Dalziel, 2014). 45. An analysis for the Global Action Report on Preterm Birth estimated that achieving universal coverage (95%) of antenatal corticosteroids across 75 priority countries by 2015 could avert 373,000 additional infant deaths annually compared to 2010 figures (March of Dimes, 2012). 46. Caution has been advised in scaling up antenatal corticosteroid administration, particularly in low-income countries where access to other effective interventions, such as accurate pregnancy dating and neonatal resuscitation, may be limited (Lawn, 2013). 47. A single course of antenatal corticosteroids has been identified as a highly effective and safe intervention for women at risk of preterm birth to reduce neonatal mortality and morbidity (Crowley, 1990; Roberts, 2006). 48. The benefits of antenatal corticosteroids were first described in a landmark trial conducted in New Zealand by Liggins and Howie in the late 1960s (Liggins, 1972). 49. Subsequent clinical trials and systematic reviews have confirmed the efficacy of antenatal corticosteroids in significantly reducing the risk of RDS, neonatal death, IVH, NEC, and early sepsis (Crowley, 1990; Roberts, 2006). 50. Evidence suggests that in infants born more than seven days after antenatal corticosteroid treatment, there is no reduction in the incidence of RDS compared to no treatment (Roberts, 2006). 51. Repeat antenatal corticosteroids have been administered to women who remain at risk of preterm birth seven or more days after an initial course. 52. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that repeat doses of synthetic corticosteroids, such as betamethasone, are associated with reduced risks of RDS and combined serious neonatal morbidity compared to a single course (Crowther, 2015). 53. However, uncertainty remains regarding the effects of repeat antenatal corticosteroids on reduced birth weight and long-term outcomes in childhood and later life following repeated in utero exposure (Crowther, 2015). 54. Long-term follow-up of infants exposed to a single course of antenatal corticosteroids into early adulthood has not demonstrated increased cardio-metabolic risk (Dalziel, 2005; Dessens, 2000). 55. Follow-up studies of infants up to early school age after repeat antenatal corticosteroid exposure have been reassuring (Asztalos, 2010; Asztalos, 2013; Crowther, 2007; McKinlay, 2015; Peltonemi, 2009; Wapner, 2007). 56. The long-term effects of repeat corticosteroids on growth, the neuroendocrine system, and the risk of developing cardiovascular and metabolic diseases in later life remain unknown (Crowther, 2015). 57. Antenatal corticosteroids have been administered prior to elective cesarean sections to minimize the risk of respiratory distress at late preterm and term gestations (Stutchfield, 2005; Tita, 2009). 58. Infants born by cesarean section at term are at greater risk of respiratory morbidity, including transient tachypnea of the newborn and RDS, compared to term infants born vaginally (Hansen, 2008; Morrison, 1995; Sotiriadis, 2009). 59. Limited data exist on the long-term effects of antenatal corticosteroid exposure prior to cesarean section at term. 60. The two main synthetic corticosteroids used in clinical practice are betamethasone and dexamethasone (NIH, 1994; PMNCH, 2011; RCOG, 2010; ACS CPG, 2015). 61. Despite widespread use, there is significant global variation in the type, preparation, dose, and method of administration of antenatal corticosteroids (Aleman, 2013; Erickson, 2001; Hui, 2007; Jobe, 2004; Parant, 2008; Pattanittum, 2008; Spencer, 2014; Vogel, 2014). 62. The optimal type of corticosteroid to use remains unclear (Brownfoot, 2013). 63. Both betamethasone and dexamethasone cross the placenta in their biologically active forms and exert their effects with comparable efficiency (Jobe, 2004). 64. Intramuscular betamethasone can be administered in two different drug preparations: betamethasone sodium phosphate, which has a short half-life of six hours in maternal plasma, and betamethasone acetate, which has a longer half-life of approximately 12 hours (Ballard, 1975; Buckingham, 2006). 65. Liggins and Howie initially proposed that combining these two preparations would maximize drug efficacy (Liggins, 1972). 66. Antenatal corticosteroids have been administered in various ways, including orally, intramuscularly, intravenously, intra-amniotically, and as a direct intramuscular injection to the fetus (Egerman, 1998; Liggins, 1972; Petersen, 1983; Lefebvre, 1976; Murphy, 1982; Ljubic, 1999). 67. Betamethasone and dexamethasone have been administered intramuscularly in a variety of regimens. 68. Trial regimens of a single course of antenatal betamethasone have included total doses ranging from 12 mg to 48 mg, administered in single or multiple doses at varied time intervals (immediate, eight hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours apart). 69. Trial regimens of a single course of dexamethasone have included total doses ranging from 20 mg to 24 mg, administered in multiple divided doses at varied time intervals (eight hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours apart). 70. Trials have also compared the administration of repeat courses of antenatal corticosteroids to no repeat courses. 71. Predominantly, these trials have administered betamethasone as the repeat course, apart from one trial that used dexamethasone due to the temporary unavailability of betamethasone (Garite, 2009). 72. The trial regimens of repeat antenatal betamethasone have included total doses ranging from 11.4 mg to 24 mg per repeat course, administered in single or multiple doses 24 hours apart. 73. The time interval between repeat courses and the number of repeat courses varied between trials. 74. Glucocorticoids exert physiological and biochemical effects on most fetal organ systems, not just the lungs (Fowden, 1998). 75. They promote structural and functional maturation, preparing the fetus for life outside the womb. 76. Synthetic corticosteroids induce a coordinated maturation response in fetal tissues similar to the normal pre-partum surge in fetal corticosteroid production (Liggins, 1994). 77. Experimental studies in animals and human fetal lung explants have demonstrated that exposure to corticosteroids increases surfactant production, lung compliance, fluid clearance from the lungs, maturation of parenchymal structure, and reduced vascular permeability (Ballard, 1995). 78. These effects help mitigate the consequences of preterm birth with immature lung structure and function (Ballard, 1995). 79. At a molecular level, glucocorticoids primarily act by inducing gene transcription via the glucocorticoid receptor. 80. This leads to increased concentrations of enzymes and proteins, including lung phospholipids and surfactant proteins (Ballard, 1995). 81. The reversibility of glucocorticoid action following dissociation of the steroid from the receptor and the clinical observation that corticosteroid effectiveness diminishes over time if the fetus remains in utero have led to the administration of repeat steroids to women at risk of preterm birth (Ballard, 1995; Liggins, 1972). 82. This approach was originally proposed by Liggins and Howie and has been supported by experimental data showing that gene transcription can be repeatedly induced (Ballard, 1995; Ballard, 1997; Willet, 2001). 83. Follow-up studies of children exposed to repeat antenatal corticosteroids in utero compared to unexposed children have shown no differences in mortality, neuro-sensory disability, growth, blood pressure, or respiratory morbidity (Asztalos, 2010; Asztalos, 2013; Crowther, 2007; McKinlay, 2015; Peltonemi, 2009; Wapner, 2007). 84. The pathophysiology underlying respiratory morbidity in infants born by elective cesarean section at term is thought to differ from that occurring after preterm birth (Brown, 1983). 85. A significant proportion of respiratory morbidity in term infants after cesarean delivery is due to retention of fetal lung fluid (Milner, 1978; Morrison, 1995). 86. Administration of corticosteroids prior to elective cesarean section has been proposed based on evidence that antenatal corticosteroids facilitate the clearance of fluid from the fetal lung by increasing the number and function of sodium channels (Helve, 2009; Jain, 2006). 87. The precise mechanism has not been confirmed, and the long-term consequences of administration on child and adult health outcomes have not been established. 88. While the use of a single course of antenatal corticosteroids prior to preterm birth is widely accepted as one of the most effective interventions in perinatal medicine, several aspects of administration remain uncertain, including their use in late preterm and term gestations, repeat dosing, optimal drug formulation, route and timing of administration, and use in different healthcare settings. 89. This overview aims to clarify these uncertainties, identify the health benefits and potential harms associated with antenatal corticosteroid administration, and highlight areas for future high-quality randomized trials. 90. Ultimately, this overview seeks to provide a user-friendly, comprehensive source of current evidence from Cochrane systematic reviews to encourage the appropriate administration of antenatal corticosteroids to all eligible mothers and their babies.
